title: The dimension of self-similar measures
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: The course is an exposition, with a complete proof, of OpenAI's theorem (2026) that a self-similar measure on the line has the dimension min(1, h/chi), where h is the entropy rate of the random walk of composed maps and chi the mean logarithmic contraction, without any separation assumption. The proof assumes that the measure is exact dimensional (a named hypothesis, a theorem of Feng and Hu that the course does not prove), and the course states the theorem for the exact dimension d. The first lesson proves the rules for entropies of random variables with finitely many values that the proof uses: the chain rule, conditioning, mutual information, mixtures, and two estimates for the binary entropy. The second lesson defines the entropy of a law on the line at a scale s, averaged over the positions of a grid of length s, and proves its rules: invariance under translations and the rule for scaling; comparison of two scales; for an integer ratio of scales, the difference of the entropies is a mean of conditional entropies, lies between 0 and log N, is concave in the law (also for measurable mixtures) and does not decrease under convolution; and the identity that adding a uniform choice among K steps of length v changes the scale from v to Kv. The third lesson defines self-similar measures (existence, uniqueness, decomposition along stopped words), states exact dimensionality as the named hypothesis (ED), proves that the entropy at scale s of an exact-dimensional law of dimension d is at most (d + o(1)) log(1/s), and proves uniform nonsaturation: for a self-similar measure of dimension less than one the one-bit deficit is bounded below by a positive constant at all scales. The fourth lesson proves the two-point gain (replacing every point of a bounded law by a fair pair of size v raises the entropy between scales s < v < t by at least the one-bit deficit at scale v minus s/v and v/t), defines the pair capacities of a finite law, and proves that a convolution gains entropy from the fair pairs contained in one factor. The fifth lesson proves the pair bound for a finite law: k times the entropy inside the cells of length rho is at most log |kF| plus 53760 k^4 times the sum of the pair capacities at scales below 2 rho, with a constant that does not depend on the distances in the support; the proof uses random nested partitions. The sixth lesson defines the walk of maps G_n, its entropy rate h and the exponent chi, proves that the entropy at scale s of an exact-dimensional law is (d + o(1)) log(1/s), and proves the upper bound d <= min(1, h/chi) for a self-similar measure that is exact dimensional with dimension d. The seventh lesson assumes d chi < h, groups the symbols into blocks, conditions on the types of the blocks (the numbers of occurrences of each symbol), and proves that the finite laws of the translations of the maps of n blocks have a total pair capacity of at least c n in a finite range of scales finer than 2^(-An). The eighth lesson completes the proof of the dimension formula d = min(1, h/chi) for every self-similar measure on the line that is exact dimensional: under d < 1 and d chi < h, the pairs of stretches of blocks give gains of entropy in windows of scales that, at each scale, come from disjoint stretches and add up to at most 2 log M, while the number of bands is arbitrary; it also proves the formula d = min(1, H(p)/chi) without exact overlaps. The whole proof is in the course; it assumes exact dimensionality (the named hypothesis (ED)).
prerequisites: core course Measure and Integration (D10): the Lebesgue integral of bounded measurable functions, measurable families of measures, exchange of two integrals of nonnegative functions
finite sums, the natural logarithm and the inequality ln x <= x - 1; the lessons prove every other fact they use

checks.reading: The manuscript 'The entropy-rate dimension formula for self-similar measures on the line' (OpenAI, 24 Sep 2026) was read in full on 12 Oct 2026 (six sections, 1,576 lines of TeX); a first-pass check of its steps is recorded in plan/OPENAI_148_SCOPING_20261012.md. Lesson 1 contains the rules of entropy that the manuscript uses without proof ('the entropy chain rule and nonnegativity of conditional mutual information'), and the two estimates for the binary entropy that it uses in the proofs of uniform nonsaturation (strong concavity, constant 1/(2 ln 2)) and of the pair bound (h_2(q) <= 3 sqrt(q)). All statements are standard; each proof was written out and checked by hand. Lesson 2 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against the lemma 'Entropy calculus' of Section 2. The lesson proves all its statements with sums over grid cells; the manuscript's identity H_s(X) = h(X + V_s) - log s with differential entropy is replaced by its discrete form H_v(X + v U) = H_{Kv}(X) + log K (Proposition 3.1), which gives Delta_v as an averaged mutual information without densities. Concavity is proved for measurable mixtures by a Jensen inequality on a simplex, proved in the lesson. Checked numerically before staging (plan/checks_20261012/sd_check_scale.py): the two worked examples (two atoms; the uniform law, H_{1/n} = log n + 1/(2n ln 2)); Proposition 3.1 on 12 random finite laws (deviation 3e-4, the integration error); the two-sided comparison of scales; the convolution inequality. Two exercises of a first draft had unverified solutions and were replaced by verified ones before staging. Lesson 3 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against the lemmas 'Entropy and dimension' and 'Uniform nonsaturation' of Section 2 and the definitions of Section 1. Every step was derived. The manuscript's argument with densities of X + V_v and total variation is carried out with laws of grid cells: Lemma 3.1 (||p - Tp||^2 <= 2 ln 2 I(J; F + J)), Lemma 3.2 (I(U; F + U) <= K(K-1)/2 ||p - Tp|| log K, by a common part and an independent flag), Proposition 3.3 with the constant made explicit. Checked numerically before staging (plan/checks_20261012/sd_check_nonsat.py): the three inequalities on 4,000 random laws; Delta_v for the Cantor measure at thirty scales (between 0.36 and 0.40) and for the uniform law (1/(4n ln 2)). No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 4 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against the lemma 'Two-point gain' of Section 2, the definition of pair capacity in Section 3, and the step of the proof of the lemma 'Conditional pair gain' in Section 5 that applies concavity to the selected pairs and the residual measure. Every step was derived. The identity D_v = Delta_v is taken from Corollary 3.2 of the second lesson, in place of the manuscript's differential entropies. The coarse-scale bound D_t <= v/t is proved by conditioning on the two labels of X and X + v, which have finitely many values, in place of conditioning on X. Theorem 2.3 states the deterministic content of the manuscript's use of pairs as a separate result. Checked numerically before staging (plan/checks_20261012/sd_check_twopoint.py): D_v = Delta_v, D_s >= D_v - s/v, D_t <= v/t and the two-point gain on 14 random laws and scales; the gain from pairs on 8 random convolutions; largest deviation 2.2e-4 with integration over 3,000 shifts. No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 5 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Section 3 (the lemma 'Finite-law pair bound'), the estimate that the manuscript presents as its new tool. Every line of the proof was derived again: the lengths and number of children of the random partitions and the density of a cut (20/rho_h); the chain over the levels; the step after the sum is observed (at most one exceptional coordinate forces a deviation of the sum of more than a/2; flag only for the event of two exceptions; h_2(q) <= 3 sqrt(q) <= 3t); the average over the cuts (7k cuts, probability 160 k u / rho_h each); the coupling and its bands against the pair capacities; the geometric sum 8/3. The constant comes out as 20160 * 8/3 = 53760 k^4, within the manuscript's 60000 k^4. The lesson defines the probability space of the cuts explicitly (a finite cube of independent uniform coordinates indexed by labels) and notes the Borel measurability; it treats the case a = 0 separately. Checked before staging (plan/checks_20261012/sd_check_pairbound.py): the partition geometry on 2,000 random cells; the step after the sum by exact enumeration on 3,000 random configurations with k = 1, 2, 3 (labels fixed outside E and B; both inequalities); the average over the cuts by simulation (largest observed ratio 155 against the bound 1120); the bands of the coupling against capacities computed by linear programming on 300 random laws; the whole inequality on 300 random laws; the geometric sum. No discrepancy with the manuscript and no error found in its proof. Lesson 6 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Section 1 (definitions of G_n, h and chi; the subsection on the upper bound). The manuscript proves the upper bound for the Hausdorff dimension by coverings, with the strong law of large numbers for blocks. The lesson proves it for the exact dimension d with entropies at a scale: a lower bound for the entropy of an exact-dimensional law (Proposition 2.1), the decomposition X = G_n(X') (Lemma 3.1), the bound H^0_s(mu) <= H(G_n) + log(2R_0+2) + P(|r_{G_n}| > s) log(2R_0/s+2) (Lemma 3.2) and Chebyshev's inequality (Lemma 1.3). This is a different argument from the manuscript's, chosen because the course does not use Hausdorff dimension; the statement d = dim_H for exact-dimensional measures, which the manuscript notes, is not proved or used in the course. Checked before staging (plan/checks_20261012/sd_check_upper.py): for the maps x/3, x/3+1, x/3+3 with equal weights, the numbers of distinct maps of length 1 to 9 (3, 8, 21, 55, 144, 377, 987, 2584, 6765) and H(G_n)/n by exact rational enumeration, H(G_2) = log 9 - 2/9, subadditivity; the formula of Exercise 4.2; the count of Exercise 4.3; Lemma 3.2 on a system with unequal ratios of both signs; Lemma 1.3 by exact enumeration. Lesson 7 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Section 4 (parameters; block types; the lemma 'Entropy retained by types'; the proposition 'Pair mass in finite scale bands'). Every step was derived again and holds: gamma > 0 and b chi < A' < A; the composition formula; E H(nu) = H(G_bn | Omega_n) >= n h_b; E H^0_s(nu) <= H^0_s(mu) + 1 (concavity for a measurable family of translates, then for the finite mixture over the types); the deficit of at least (gamma/4) n on the event E_n; the sumset bound log |kS| <= n m^b log(k+1); the index condition 2^-l <= 2 rho_n iff l >= a_n; the constant c = k eps / (2 C_k). The lesson works with finite tuples of types only (no infinite type sequences are needed here) and uses Chebyshev's inequality where the manuscript cites the law of large numbers. Checked before staging (plan/checks_20261012/sd_check_types.py) on two systems (one with exact overlaps; one with unequal ratios and a negative ratio) for six pairs (b, n) with b n <= 6, by exact rational enumeration: the composition formula, the two-stage description of blocks, E H(nu) = H(G_bn | Omega_n) >= H(G_bn) - H(Omega_n), the grid-entropy inequality at three scales, the sumset bound for k = 1, 2, 3, the count of types; and the parameters of the example in Section 1. No discrepancy with the manuscript and no error found. Lesson 8 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Section 5 (suffix laws, the lemma 'Conditional pair gain', the choice of separated bands, the lemma 'Disjoint retained windows', the sum over target depths, the completion of the proof) and Section 6 (overlap lengths; the corollaries for measures). Every step was derived again and holds: the suffix convolution identity; 0 <= g_j <= 2 log M and monotonicity; the scale window v/rho in [1, 4) and the error 5/M; the convexity step with the mean over the later types; the separation condition and the order of retained windows; the one-to-one correspondence between targets L and band indices; the count |J_i| n_i >= T/(2D); the bound Q <= 8 D log M / (delta c). The lesson works with a finite number N of blocks: the tail law tau_j is conditioned on the types of the blocks j to N-1 only and ends in a copy of mu, so that no law conditioned on an infinite sequence of types is needed; the identities and the monotonicity are the same. Checked before staging (plan/checks_20261012/sd_check_windows.py) on 292 random instances of the combinatorial part: disjointness of the retained windows for every target, the exact correspondence between targets and band indices, the telescoping bound, the scale window, the count; and the overlap lemma on random words. The corollary on the Hausdorff dimension of the attractor (Section 6 of the manuscript) is not in the course. No error was found in Sections 5 and 6.

open_obligations: Not in the course: the corollary of Section 6 of the manuscript on the Hausdorff dimension of the attractor without exact overlaps (dim_H K = min(1, s_*)); it needs Hausdorff dimension of sets, which the course does not introduce. The main theorem and the corollaries for measures are in the course with complete proofs, under the named hypothesis (ED).

Named hypothesis (ED) of the third lesson: every self-similar measure on the line (finitely many maps r_i x + t_i with 0 < |r_i| < 1, positive weights, no separation assumption) is exact dimensional. This is the theorem of D.-J. Feng and H. Hu (2009) as cited in the manuscript; it has not been read for this course and the programme has no proof of it. Theorem 3.5 of the third lesson assumes exact dimensionality explicitly.

Not proved and not used in the course: for an exact-dimensional measure the exact dimension d equals the Hausdorff dimension of the measure (the infimum of the Hausdorff dimensions of the Borel sets of positive measure). The course states its results for d; the manuscript states them for the Hausdorff dimension.
